newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Industry calls for action on Colombia port strike.
newsitem.headline: Industry calls for action on Colombia port strike.

text.p: Colombia's powerful National Industrial Association (ANDI) called on the government Thursday to take a "decisive and efficient" hand in ending the dockworkers' strike at the country's main Pacific coast port.
It said the nine-day-old stoppage at the port of Buenaventura was a "grave threat to the national economy" and was creating widespread international uncertainty.

Talks aimed at ending the strike deadlock resumed at 1100 local/1600 GMT Thursday in the provincial capital Cali. Negotiations progressed well through much of Wednesday afternoon but were suspended in the early hours Thursday as dockworkers, ship owners and cargo operators failed to agree on a minimum price for handling sugar consignments, a union representative said.
The port is the shipment point for about 60 percent of Colombian coffee exports and all its sugar exports.
"The Buenaventura strike has paralyzed the normal development of foreign trade, is threatening the national economy and has generated international uncertainty," ANDI said in a statement.

"We call on the ministers of the interior, labor and foreign trade to intervene in a decisive and efficient manner...to ensure there's a quick solution to the conflict without risk to the stability and the future of the Colombian port system," it added.
National Coffee Growers' Federation and private exporters say more than 300,000 60-kg bags of coffee have been snarled in the strike.

The federation only began authorizing exporters Wednesday to start pulling truck loads of coffee out of Buenaventura and redirecting them to Caribbean coast ports. This could delay shipments until at least Feb 2, a private exporter said.
Port authorities said at least 27,000 tonnes of sugar, in sacks and bulk containers, were blocked in port.

A spokesman added that 15 ships were laying idle in port and 28 others had been diverted to Guayaquil, Ecuador, or Balboa, Panama, since the strike began, leading to a loss of 5,000 containers and 60,000 tonnes of other cargo. He said the port was losing about $1 million a day for every day the stoppage lasted.

The industrial action has contributed to a heavy rise in coffee prices and some New York-based brokers said rumors were sweeping the market that the Colombian military was about to intervene to break up the strike.
Jose Felix Grueso, general secretary of Buenaventura city hall, said there had been no hint of military intervention.
"There are no public order problems. The strike has been conducted with great dignity," he said. The city mayor and the state governor are both mediating the strike talks.

Gruso said the livelihoods of about 10,000 people depended directly on the port activities in Buenaventura. He argued that since the port was privatized in 1993, the dock workers have seen wage levels plummet, to an average of less than $80 per month, adding that unemployment had soared to 60 percent, above the national average of about 11.5 percent.
